items.title: George Lewis Interview, 1968-11-01
items.q: I played with that band the whole tree nights at Empire. And, uh, when I came back that morning, but it was dead.

ctx.x: But were you playing with this band down in that band?

I played with that band the whole tree nights at Empire. And, uh, when I came back that morning, but it was dead. Because he missed one of them nights. He took a ciggy. He went on across the right opposite. He was chasing. He had a speakeasy. And, uh, you went in that speakeasy and he'd done a lot of drinking. I mean.
This was an empire. No, no. He came from the last job. You mean the speakeasy was on St. Philip? On St. Philip, right. Opposite to the way he is. Yeah.

items.title: George Lewis Interview, 1968-10-21
items.q: a few pieces that we played in there with Buddy P. D.

ctx.x: Uh huh. But I was lucky, like, a few pieces that we played in there with Buddy P. D. like, uh, Maverly Prahm. So he had to switch his corner to a low key. And that would make a lot of fellas couldn't cross. But I would look at a few pieces that we played in there with Buddy P. D. like, uh, uh, and then he would come in. Maple Leaf Rag. Those kind of numbers. I'd push my car like he would, but I had to play in a different key. See the trumpet, if he's playing in the key of Bb, I'm playing the same key as the…
You played, um, that number, whatever you said, in A's?

items.title: George Lewis Interview, 1958-11-14
items.q: I tried to take Edmund Hall, plays with Buddy Petit when Edmund Hall left.

ctx.x: Did you hear Edmund Hall over there?
Yes. I tried to take Edmund Hall, plays with Buddy Petit when Edmund Hall left.
Did he play the same as he plays now? Almost. Almost. Would Zeb have a tone like him or more like yours? Zeb had a tone more like Edmund Hall. What about Georgie Boyd? What kind of tone did he have?
Well, people engaged here more than us. People saw... stuff

I don't know anybody who would be the best friend, but you didn't get the opportunity to get off. That's when you were. Did you hear Johnny Dawes when you were married? I was Johnny Dawes. I was Johnny, I was Jimmy Newman, Charlie McQuirties, and he was one of the best. I was the man George Backing, he was one of the best. I was his brother. He was a kid, he was a kid. The first funeral I played with Eddie Jackson was on this side of the river. I was working with Eddie Jackson at what they call a music hall. I…

But he couldn't play no more. He was way up, way up by the protection of the levy. And he'd see you sick. He'd have that coat on, that cap, as I must care for you. He loved his music. He was a bass player. John Smith was a pimp. He had a lot of women dressed very good. He was in Ace Blossom, one of the Zulus Club. He was a band-girl. Wood-Jill Trump, sometimes called him. Sometimes he was a friend I named Homer. He lived on the main. Jetson was called the same block as the high court. He was in Jetson. He signed…
